column4: After the murdered man is struck with part of the cow, God brings him to life; the verse explicitly says God thus brings the dead to life, a narrated instance of the section’s death-to-life movement.

The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes something becoming existent after nonexistence; this verse says God originates the heavens and earth and that when He decrees a thing, it is. It makes that coming-into-being a divine act.
The verse says not to call those killed in God’s path dead, for they are alive with their Lord. It reverses the funeral status at the center of the section; 3:169 gives a parallel formulation.
The verse describes the waiting period of wives after their husbands die; it gives a concrete life of separation after death, corresponding to the section’s note that farewell extends to the dead.
A people flee death, God tells them to die, then gives them life; this is a collective death-and-return scene, though it does not depict burial.

The section title uses tabut for a funeral chest; this verse’s التابوت is the covenant chest carrying tranquility and relics, not a corpse. The shared container image marks a specific boundary between the funerary bier and the Ark.
A man is made to die for a hundred years and then revived, while the bones of his donkey are reassembled. This gives a concrete case of bodily death and renewed life after decay.
Jesus says he brings the dead to life by God’s permission; this is a direct scene of death followed by restored life.
The verse says every soul tastes death and receives its full reward on the Day of Resurrection; it joins mortality to the life and judgment that follow.

The section notes that an orphan’s status carries the death of a father; this verse protects the property of orphans, giving a concrete consequence of that parental loss, though it does not narrate the death.
The verse orders guardians to test orphans until maturity and then hand over their property; it develops the practical aftermath of the father’s death implicit in orphanhood.
In God’s address to Jesus, raising the dead by God’s permission is recalled among the signs given him; it repeats the section’s passage from death to life in a narrated miracle.
The section’s dictionary form for و ج د names existence after nonexistence; here God says that when He wills a thing, He commands it and it is, a specific formulation of coming into being.
After the question about bones in 17:49, this verse asks who will bring the deniers back and answers: the One who created them the first time. It supplies the first-creation argument for return.
The human asks whether he will be brought out alive after he has died; this is a direct question about life after death, continuing the creation-from-nothing discussion in 19:67.
The verse says God will repeat creation as He began it, comparing the Day to a scroll rolled up; it directly states second creation and adds the image of a written record.
Following the earth and human-creation signs in 22:5, this verse states that God is true and gives life to the dead; it makes the resurrection claim explicit.
The verse says every soul tastes death and then returns to God, a direct formulation of the death-to-return movement in the section.
The verse points to dead earth revived by rain and says God is capable of all things; it gives another specific earth-after-death analogy for the section’s renewed-life theme.
After the new-creation question in 34:7, this verse locates the accusers in disbelief in the Hereafter and error; it identifies the stance behind their resistance to renewed existence.
The verse says God gives life to the dead and records what people send ahead and their traces; it joins resurrection to what remains of a person’s actions.
After the answer about reviving bones in 36:79, this verse asks whether the Creator of the heavens and earth can create their like; it adds the scale-of-creation argument for re-creation.

The section’s dictionary form for و ج د describes what comes to exist after not existing; this verse says that when God wills a thing, it is by His command, giving another explicit formulation of origination.
The verse joins giving life and death to God’s command that a thing exist when He decrees it; it connects the image’s death-to-life passage with creation by divine command.
The verse argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can give life to the dead; it directly supports the section’s transition from death to renewed existence.
The verse describes God bringing grain from dead land and providing for His servants; in the same surah that says the earth diminishes bodies, it gives an earth-revival counterpart to resurrection.
The verse asks whether the first creation exhausted God, then says the deniers remain confused about a new creation; it directly contests the same second-creation question as 32:10.
The passage begins its death scene when the soul reaches the throat; it supplies the moment of departure that precedes the section’s shroud, farewell, and burial image.
The verse says the onlookers are watching as the soul reaches the throat in 56:83; it adds the witnesses present at death before the ensuing challenge about return.
The verse says God is nearer to the dying person than the watching people, though they do not see; it locates divine presence in the death scene begun in 56:83.
After the soul reaches the throat in 56:83, the verse challenges the onlookers to return it if they are not answerable to God; it makes the limit between death and human power explicit.
The next verse completes the challenge in 56:86: if the onlookers are truthful, they should return the soul. Its contribution is the final impossibility in this death scene.
The verse depicts the soul reaching the collarbones, the threshold of death; it gives the section’s farewell and burial image the preceding moment of bodily departure.
As death arrives in 75:26, people ask who can cure or save the dying person; this verse adds the futile appeal at the point of departure.
The next verse says the dying person knows it is the moment of separation; it makes farewell explicit within the death scene begun in 75:26.
The verse describes the legs being joined as death advances, continuing the bodily scene of departure before the return to God in 75:30.
The verse says that day the person is driven to his Lord; it completes the death sequence in 75:26–29 with the movement to divine return.
After describing human creation and development, the verse asks whether God cannot give life to the dead; it states the section’s renewed-life claim as the conclusion of a creation argument.

After asking whether a time passed when the human was nothing in 76:1, this verse says God created the human from a mixed drop and tested him; it completes the passage from nonexistence to embodied life.
